624.title: Neither coming nor going
624.hook: a sphere where there is no earth, water, fire or wind, no coming or going
624.howItsDone: This passage is often read in Theravada teaching on nibbana, and some meditation teachers cite it when explaining that the goal is not a meditative state or a heavenly place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four words that begin with un. Your line: because there is, an escape is known. Today, the saying that opens the same chapter.
screen: `BECAUSE THERE IS, AN ESCAPE IS KNOWN.`

segments.voice: Try to describe silence without mentioning sound. Or darkness without mentioning light. It's almost impossible; people describe things by what's in them. The first discourse of the Udana's last chapter takes on an even harder job. The Buddha is instructing the monks about nibbana, and the text says they listen with their whole minds, paying close attention, ears open. What he gives them is not a description. It's a list of everything that isn't there.
screen: `DESCRIBE SILENCE WITHOUT SOUND.` → `THE MONKS LISTEN CLOSELY.` → `A LIST OF WHAT ISN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: There is, monks, that sphere, he says, where there is no earth, no water, no fire, no wind. Those four elements were the ancient way of naming everything solid, liquid, hot and moving: everything physical. None of it there. Then he goes further. Not the sphere of infinite space, not infinite consciousness, not nothingness, not neither-perception-nor-non-perception: the four formless states the texts describe, very subtle places a meditating mind can reach. Not those either. Not this world, not another world, not sun, not moon. There, he says, there is no coming, no going, no staying, no passing away, no arising. It has no support, no movement, no basis. This, just this, is the end of dukkha. Yesterday's saying named the unborn. Today's empties out every place you might look for it, from the ground under your feet to the highest heaven of the mind. And then, after all those nots, one word of yes: this is the end of suffering. Theravada teachers read the passage as describing nibbana, which isn't a place in the ordinary sense, even though the text calls it a sphere.
screen: `NO EARTH, WATER, FIRE, WIND.` · `NOT EVEN THE FORMLESS STATES.` · `NO COMING, NO GOING, NO STAYING.` · `THIS, JUST THIS.` · then, large: `THE END OF DUKKHA.`

segments.voice: Give the listening your whole mind, the way the monks did, ears open. A sound arrives; follow it until it ends, then the next, noticing that each has a coming and a going, and a gap between. Don't fill the gap with a thought; just keep listening, without reaching for anything.
Ayatana, a sphere or base. The Udana's words for nibbana: no earth, water, fire or wind; no coming, going or staying; just this, the end of dukkha. Today's word.
Your line: the end of dukkha. After all the nots, one plain yes. See you tomorrow.

625.title: No blame to Cunda
625.hook: the smith's meal, and the Buddha's care that he not be blamed
625.carry: for one who gives, merit grows
625.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell of Cunda's meal as an example of the Buddha's compassion at the end of his life, and tradition identifies the meal before the awakening as Sujata's offering of milk-rice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no earth, no water, no coming or going. Your line: the end of dukkha. Today, from the same chapter, a very human worry.

A cook makes dinner for a guest she admires. That night the guest gets sick. Even if the food had nothing to do with it, the cook lies awake. Was it the fish? Should I have known? And if the guest died, that question could follow her for years. On day eighty-one you heard about Cunda, the smith's son at Pava, who served the Buddha his last meal. The Udana tells the same story in its eighth chapter, and keeps a detail that's easy to pass over: what the Buddha did about Cunda's feelings, while he himself was dying.
screen: `DINNER, THEN SICKNESS.` → `WAS IT THE FISH?` → `CUNDA, THE SMITH'S SON.`

segments.voice: Cunda invites the Buddha and the monks for a meal, and among the dishes is one called sukaramaddava. Nobody today knows for certain what it was. Its name has the word for pig in it. The commentaries take it as tender pork; other readers have taken it as a kind of mushroom, or a herbal preparation. The text doesn't say. The Buddha tells Cunda to serve that dish to him alone, and to bury what's left, since no one else could digest it. After the meal, a severe illness comes on him, with sharp pains. He bears it, mindful, and travels on toward Kusinara. And on the road, sick and near the end, he thinks of Cunda. Someone, he tells Ananda, might make Cunda feel remorse: it's your loss, Cunda, that the Teacher passed away after eating your food. So go and dispel it. Tell him this, from me: two offerings of food bring equal and great fruit, more than any others. The meal after which the Teacher awoke, and the meal after which he passes into final release. Cunda's act was good; it brings long life, beauty, happiness and honor. Look at the care in that. Dying, the Buddha spends some of his last strength protecting a man from guilt that wasn't his. The verse says it plainly: for one who gives, merit grows.

segments.voice: Think of someone who might be blaming themselves for something that isn't really their fault: a parent, a coworker, a friend after a bad day, maybe even you. 626.title: Thus it was said
626.hook: 112 short teachings, remembered by the laywoman Khujjuttara, a servant of the queen
626.carry: she came back with something better
626.howItsDone: The Itivuttaka is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya and is read and taught in Theravada communities; Khujjuttara is honored as a model of the learned lay disciple.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the smith's meal. Your line: for one who gives, merit grows. The Udana is behind us; today, the third of the short books.

In the city of Kosambi, the story goes, Queen Samavati gives her servant money every day to buy flowers. And every day the servant, a woman named Khujjuttara, keeps some of the money for herself. Then one day she hears the Buddha teach, and she comes home with the full amount, and all the flowers it buys. The queen notices. Khujjuttara confesses. And then the queen asks her for something far more valuable than flowers.
screen: `MONEY FOR FLOWERS.` → `ONE DAY, THE FULL AMOUNT.` → `SOMETHING MORE VALUABLE.`

segments.voice: The queen and her women, the commentary says, couldn't leave the palace to hear the Buddha. So they asked Khujjuttara to go for them, and to bring the teaching home. She went, she listened, and she came back and taught them, word for word, what she'd heard. The collection that tradition says grew from her memory is the Itivuttaka. Its name means thus it was said. Every one of its 112 short discourses opens with the same humble line: this was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I heard. Not I say. Not the Buddha says. This was said, and I heard it: the voice of someone passing on what they were given, carefully, without adding. The teachings are arranged by number: a section of ones, of twos, of threes, of fours. Each is short, a few lines of prose, then verse that says it again. Khujjuttara's name means the hunchbacked Uttara, and she was a servant. Yet in the canon's list of outstanding disciples, she is named foremost among laywomen who had heard much. In the tradition's telling, the person who kept these teachings wasn't a monk or a scholar or a queen. She was the woman sent to buy flowers.
screen: `THE QUEEN COULDN'T GO.` · `SHE BROUGHT IT HOME, WORD FOR WORD.` · `THIS WAS SAID, SO I HEARD.` · `FOREMOST OF THE LEARNED.` · then, large: `THUS IT WAS SAID.`

segments.voice: Think of one good thing someone taught you, a sentence, a habit, a way of seeing, that has stayed with you, and let the face of the person who said it come to mind. Notice that you're a link in a chain, holding something that was handed to you, the way Khujjuttara carried the teachings home.
Itivuttaka. Thus it was said: 112 short teachings, each opening with this was said, so I heard, kept, tradition says, by the servant Khujjuttara. Today's word.
Your line: she came back with something better. Not only flowers, but the teaching, word for word. See you tomorrow.

627.title: Just one thing
627.hook: abandon greed, just that one thing, and I guarantee the fruit
627.carry: pull it up by the root
627.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often name greed, hatred and delusion as the three roots of unwholesome action, and some practitioners work with one of them at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khujjuttara and the flower money. Your line: she came back with something better. Today, the very first teaching in her book.

Self-help shelves are full of lists. Seven habits. Twelve rules. Thirty days to a better you. Lists are useful, and Buddhist texts love them too: four truths, eight factors, five hindrances. But sometimes a list is a way of putting things off; there's always one more item to read about before starting. The Itivuttaka opens with no list at all. Its section of ones begins with a single thing, and an unusual promise. The Buddha doesn't say try this. He says: I guarantee it.
screen: `SEVEN HABITS, TWELVE RULES.` → `A LIST CAN BE A DELAY.` → `ONE THING, AND A GUARANTEE.`

segments.voice: Here is the first teaching of the book, after the opening line. Abandon one thing, monks, and I am your guarantee of non-return. What one thing? Greed. Non-return is a technical term: in the early texts, the third of four stages of awakening, someone who won't be reborn in this world of the senses again. So the promise is enormous, and the condition is one thing. The verse explains: driven by greed, beings go to a bad destination; seeing greed rightly, those who understand let it go, and having let it go, they don't come back to this world. Then the very next teachings say the same, one at a time. Abandon one thing: hatred. Then delusion. Then anger, then contempt, then conceit. Each one alone, with the same guarantee. Why would one be enough? The text doesn't say. One way teachers explain it: these aren't six separate weeds; pull one up by the root, really by the root, and the others turn out to grow from the same soil. And the word guarantee: the Pali, patibhoga, means a guarantor, someone who stands surety. In the text, the Buddha puts his own word behind the promise.
screen: `ABANDON ONE THING: GREED.` · `NON-RETURN, THE THIRD STAGE.` · `HATRED, DELUSION, ANGER, CONCEIT.` · `I STAND AS YOUR GUARANTEE.` · then, large: `JUST ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Ask where a little greed shows up in your day: a second helping you don't want, checking a price again, wanting the last word. Choose just one small one, picture the moment it usually happens, and picture yourself letting it go, hand open, breath out.
Lobha, greed. The opening of the Itivuttaka: abandon this, just that, and the Buddha stands as your guarantee. Today's word.

628.title: Share even the last bite
628.hook: if beings knew the result of giving, they would not eat without sharing
628.howItsDone: In many Buddhist homes a portion of food is set aside or offered before eating, and giving food to monks, neighbors and those in need is among the most common daily acts of generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abandon greed, just that. Your line: pull it up by the root. Today, the same book shows what the open hand does next.

Two kids, one cookie left. Watch what happens. Usually it's a negotiation: who had more, who's bigger, who asked first. And sometimes, rarely, one of them just breaks it and hands over half without being asked. Grown-ups do the same math with bigger things. On day one hundred thirty-four you met this teaching from the Itivuttaka: if people knew, they'd share. Today, read it closer, and listen for three small words in the middle of it: as I know.
screen: `TWO KIDS, ONE COOKIE.` → `WHO HAD MORE?` → `THREE SMALL WORDS: AS I KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the teaching. If beings knew, as I know, the result of giving and sharing, dana and samvibhaga, they would not eat without having given, and the stain of stinginess would not take hold of their minds. Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing it, if there were someone to receive it. But because beings don't know, as I know, they eat without having given, and the stain of stinginess takes hold. Now the phrase: as I know. The Buddha isn't saying be nicer. He's saying the problem is not knowing. If you could really see what giving does, to the receiver and to the giver, you wouldn't need to be told; you'd just do it, the way you'd step out of the rain. Stinginess, in this teaching, is a kind of blindness, and the word for it is a stain, something that clouds the mind. Notice the small realism at the end: if there were someone to receive it. Nobody is asked to throw food away to prove a point. It's about the moment when there's someone in front of you. And notice the scale. Not a fortune. A mouthful, about as small as a gift can be. Even there, the hand can open.

segments.voice: Remember a time someone shared food with you when they didn't have much, a grandparent, a stranger, a friend splitting a sandwich, and feel what it did for you then. 629.title: The moon outshines
629.hook: all merit-making is not worth a sixteenth part of metta, as starlight to moonlight
629.howItsDone: Metta practice is taught in Theravada communities and in other Buddhist schools; practitioners often begin with someone easy to love and widen the wish of goodwill step by step to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: if beings knew, as I know. Your line: notice who it feeds. Today, the very next teaching sets something above even generosity.

Go outside on a clear night far from city lights, and the stars are astonishing, the whole sky crowded. Then the full moon rises. As it climbs, the fainter stars fade out. They're all still there. The moon just outshines them. The Itivuttaka uses that exact sight. Yesterday it praised giving as something people would never skip if they understood it. Right after, it says there's something brighter still.
screen: `A SKY CROWDED WITH STARS.` → `THEN THE FULL MOON RISES.` → `SOMETHING BRIGHTER STILL.`

segments.voice: Whatever grounds there are for making merit, the Buddha says, giving, offerings, good works of every kind, all of them together are not worth a sixteenth part of the mind's release through metta, loving-kindness. Metta outshines them; it shines and glows and blazes. Then three pictures. As the light of all the stars together is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon's light. As in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the sky is clear, the sun rising into the sky drives away all the darkness. As at the end of the night, the morning star shines and glows and blazes. Not worth a sixteenth part: a tiny fraction. Notice what's being compared. Giving is good; yesterday's teaching made that clear, and nothing here takes it back. But giving is something you do. Metta, here, is something you become: a mind that wishes well to every being, without measure. One way to hear it: the gift is one star, and the heart it comes from is the moon. And the verse at the end: one who develops metta has their fetters wear thin. Even toward one being, loving-kindness makes a person good. Toward all beings, with a kind heart, the noble one makes abundant merit.
screen: `NOT A SIXTEENTH PART OF METTA.` · `THE STARS AND THE MOON.` · `THE AUTUMN SUN, THE MORNING STAR.` · `THE GIFT AND THE HEART IT COMES FROM.` · then, large: `THE MOON OUTSHINES.`

segments.voice: Start with one being who is easy to love, a child, a friend, a pet, and wish them well: may you be well, may you be happy. Then let it widen, to the people in this building, this street, this city, and wider, without forcing; the moon doesn't strain to shine. When the mind wanders, come back to that first easy face, and begin again.
Metta, loving-kindness. Itivuttaka 27: all merit-making together is not worth a sixteenth part of this, as starlight is to the moon. Today's word.

630.title: Two bright guardians
630.hook: conscience and concern for consequences protect the world
630.howItsDone: Theravada teachers often call hiri and ottappa the guardians of the world (lokapala dhamma), and they are counted among the wholesome qualities in Abhidhamma lists and in many Buddhist teachings on ethics.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stars fading as the moon rose. Your line: let goodwill rise first. Today closes a week, with two quiet protectors.

A driver backs out in an empty parking lot and scrapes a parked car. Nobody saw. There's no camera. She could drive away. And yet something stops her hand on the gear shift. Maybe it's a feeling: I'm not someone who does that. Maybe it's a thought: what happens to them, and to me, if I do? There's no police officer in that moment. Something inside is keeping watch. The Itivuttaka names two of those inner guards, and calls them bright.
screen: `A SCRAPE IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `NOBODY SAW.` → `SOMETHING INSIDE KEEPS WATCH.`

segments.voice: Two bright qualities, the Buddha says, protect the world. Which two? Hiri and ottappa. They're hard to translate. Hiri is often rendered moral shame or conscience: the inward sense that this act is beneath me. Ottappa is moral dread, or concern for consequences: the outward sense of what this act would do, and how it would look to the wise. One looks in, one looks out. If these two did not protect the world, the text says, people would no longer honor the bonds that hold families and communities together, not mother, not aunt, not a teacher's wife, and the world would fall into confusion. But because they guard the world, those bonds are recognized. Notice the word bright. In the early texts, sukka, bright, is used for wholesome qualities, as dark is for unwholesome ones. These aren't the gnawing, sticky guilt that keeps a person up at night. Hiri and ottappa, as teachers often explain them, look forward, and stop the hand before the harm. And notice the scale: the world, not just my peace of mind. Look back at the week. Neither coming nor going. No blame to Cunda. Thus it was said. Just one thing. Share even the last bite. The moon outshines. Most of them turned toward other people: a smith, a servant, a last bite, a wish for every being. Today's two guardians keep watch over how people treat each other.
screen: `HIRI: CONSCIENCE, LOOKING IN.` · `OTTAPPA: CONCERN, LOOKING OUT.` · `WITHOUT THEM, CONFUSION.` · `BRIGHT, NOT GNAWING GUILT.` · then, large: `TWO BRIGHT GUARDIANS.`

segments.voice: Think of a moment this week when something in you said, don't; maybe you listened, maybe you didn't, but recall the voice itself, and notice it wasn't cruel, just clear. Thank it, quietly. If an old guilt keeps gnawing, notice the difference between that and this bright guard, and let the guilt soften.
Hiri, conscience or moral shame. Paired with ottappa, concern for consequences, the two qualities the Itivuttaka says protect the world. Today's word.
Your line: listen to the small don't. Two bright guards, one looking in, one looking out. That's a week.
